title: Like stars, like dew (section 32)
hookLine: look on the world like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud (Müller, section 32)

lines: DRY BEFORE THE KEYS ARE FOUND.
cards: Dew covers the car in the driveway at six in the morning, the windshield beaded and silver. By the time the coffee's poured, the sun is over the fence, and by the time the keys are found, the glass is dry.
Nobody saw it leave. The Diamond Sutra has spent weeks cutting: self, marks, merit, views.
Now, in its last section, it stops cutting and hands over a few pictures, plain enough for a child, and says: look at the world like this.

teach.b: First, one last comparison. Someone fills worlds beyond measure with jewels and gives them all away. Someone else takes even four lines of this teaching, keeps them, and explains them to others.
The second makes the greater merit. And how should it be explained? In the sutra's own way: without taking hold of the explaining, so that it's only called explaining.

teach.h: STARS, A LAMP, DEW, A BUBBLE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Each is something you can see. Stars shine all night and fade at dawn.
A lamp burns only while the oil lasts. A magician's illusion. Dew, gone before the keys are found.
A bubble. A dream that felt like a whole life. A flash of lightning.

A cloud, changing shape as you watch. On day one hundred ninety-one, the Dhammapada asked you to look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage; here that same eye comes back. The verse doesn't say the world is fake.
Dew is really dew; it really wets the glass. A few days ago the sutra warned against hearing emptiness as nothing.
The verse holds both: real, and passing.
Then the Buddha finishes, and Subhuti, the monks and nuns, the lay men and women, gods and humans and other beings all rejoice at what he has said.
The Diamond Sutra began with an ordinary morning: a bowl, a meal, washed feet. It ends with a lamp, a bubble, and a crowd that is glad.

how: Some Mahayana communities recite the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra on its own, at the end of chanting the sutra and at other times, as a short reminder that all that is made is passing.

o: look on all that is made like stars: real, and passing
a wish that your good name will shine on forever
a saying that the dead watch over us from the sky

games.q: like dew, like lightning: tap the pairs.
p: shine all night, fade at dawn
burns only while the oil lasts

s: the closing verse says the world is fake
it says to look on all that is made like dew or lightning: real, and passing.
the sutra ends with the whole assembly rejoicing
Subhuti, monks and nuns, lay people, gods and humans rejoice at the Buddha's words.
in section 32 the jewels finally win
keeping and explaining even four lines makes the greater merit.

games.q: the sutra is ending. you're asked how to explain its four lines to someone else. what does section 32 say?
o: explain them as the final truth
explain them without taking hold of the explaining
games.why: the sutra says explain them, but in its own way: without clutching, so it's only called explaining. then comes the verse.

practice: Watch something that forms and fades: bubbles rising in a fizzy glass, breath fogging a window, or, eyes closed, the breath itself as it forms, fills and goes. Let one picture from the verse sit with you, stars or dew or lightning.
Notice the thing is real while it lasts, and that it doesn't last, and hold both gently.

wordCard.voice: Like stars. The first picture in the Diamond Sutra's closing verse: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a star; the first picture in the Diamond Sutra's closing verse.

carryVoice: Your line: like dew, like lightning. Real while it lasts, and then gone. The Diamond Sutra, done.
